lead: A shell variable is a name that holds a string. The shell uses variables to keep a path, a user name, a count or any text a script needs later. Quoting decides what happens when the shell reads a variable: it may expand to its value, stay as literal text, or split into several words. Every script uses this for configuration, counters and tests.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for how the shell reads a command line.

blocks.text: A variable is a name that holds a string. The shell does not care whether the text looks like a number; COUNT=7 stores the character 7, not an integer. To assign, write NAME=Asha. There must be no spaces around the = sign. The shell reads NAME = Asha as a command called NAME with two arguments.

Read the value with $NAME or ${NAME}. The braces mark the end of the name, so ${NAME}file gives Ashafile while $NAMEfile looks for a variable called NAMEfile. Use braces whenever text follows the name.

export NAME passes the variable into child processes as an environment variable. Without export, a script started from this shell does not see NAME. readonly NAME locks the value; a later assignment fails. unset NAME removes it.

Two useful forms: ${VAR:-default} gives the value of VAR, or default when VAR is unset or empty. ${#VAR} gives the number of characters in the value. Arrays exist in Bash, but only a few universities teach them in a first shell course; treat them as advanced.

Quoting controls expansion. Single quotes keep every character literal: echo '$NAME' prints $NAME. Double quotes expand variables and command substitution, but keep the result as one word: echo "$NAME" prints the value. A backslash \ escapes the next character, so echo \$NAME prints $NAME, with the dollar sign as literal text.

Unquoted text is split into words on spaces, tabs and newlines, and patterns such as * are expanded. If NAME='Asha Rao', echo $NAME prints two words, while echo "$NAME" prints one. Quote variables in scripts unless you truly want splitting.

Command substitution runs a command and puts its standard output in place. Use $(command); the older backtick form `command` does the same and is harder to nest. For example, TODAY=$(date +%F) stores a date string.

Arithmetic expansion computes with integers: $((expression)). It supports +, -, *, / and %. Division truncates toward zero, so $((7/2)) is 3 and $((7%2)) is 1. A bare $COUNT+3 is just text: 7+3. Write $((COUNT+3)) to get 10.

Conditional tests use operators. String tests compare text: [ "$A" = "$B" ] is true when equal, [ "$A" != "$B" ] when different. [ -z "$A" ] is true when the string is empty, and [ -n "$A" ] when it is not empty. Always quote the variable inside [ ].

Numeric tests compare integers: -eq equal, -ne not equal, -lt less than, -le less than or equal, -gt greater than, -ge greater than or equal. Write [ "$COUNT" -eq 7 ]. The string form = would compare the characters, so "05" = "5" is false while "05" -eq 5 is true.

File tests check the file system: -f path is true for a regular file, -d for a directory, -r readable, -w writable, -x executable. They are used with if, case and loops; Chapter 3.3 shows the control-flow syntax. Spaces around [ and ] and around each operator are required.
These operators are the vocabulary of decisions: compare a count, test a string, or check that a file exists before reading it.

figure.caption: The script sets NAME and COUNT, then runs four echoes in order. Notice that single quotes leave the dollar signs as text, while the arithmetic line computes 7 + 3 and prints 10.

spec.title: Worked example: four echoes
spec.aria: A script sets NAME to Asha and COUNT to 7, then four echo lines print Asha has 7, $NAME has $COUNT, 10, and 4 in order.

examples.question:
A script contains these lines. Give the exact output of each echo command, and state the two numeric results.
NAME=Asha
COUNT=7
echo "$NAME has $COUNT"
echo '$NAME has $COUNT'
echo $((COUNT+3))
echo ${#NAME}
steps: NAME=Asha stores the four-character string Asha. No spaces appear around =.
echo "$NAME has $COUNT": double quotes expand both variables, so output is Asha has 7.
echo '$NAME has $COUNT': single quotes block expansion, so output is $NAME has $COUNT.
echo $((COUNT+3)): arithmetic expansion reads COUNT as 7, adds 3, and gives 10.
echo ${#NAME}: the length of Asha is 4 characters, so output is 4.
examples.answer: The four output lines are Asha has 7, $NAME has $COUNT, 10 and 4; the arithmetic result is 10 and the string length is 4.

traps: Spaces around = turn assignment into a command: NAME = Asha does not set NAME.
An unquoted variable with spaces splits into several words; quote "$NAME" when you want one word.
= compares strings and -eq compares numbers, so "05" = "5" is false while "05" -eq 5 is true.
Single quotes block all expansion; double quotes expand variables but still keep the result as one word.

quiz.q: What does the command NAME=Asha do?
quiz.a: It assigns the string Asha to the shell variable NAME. There are no spaces around =.
It marks NAME for export so child processes receive it as an environment variable.

quiz.q: Why does echo '$HOME' print the text $HOME instead of the home directory?
quiz.a: Single quotes stop all expansion, so the shell treats $HOME as literal characters.

quiz.q: After X=12, what does echo $((X*2+1)) print?
quiz.a: Arithmetic expansion computes 12*2+1 = 25, so it prints 25.

quiz.q: A file name is stored as f="my file.txt". Why can touch $f create two files, and what is the fix?
quiz.a: Unquoted $f splits on the space into my and file.txt, so touch sees two arguments. Use touch "$f" to pass one word.

quiz.q: With N=05, compare [ "$N" -eq 5 ] and [ "$N" = 5 ]. Which is true and why?
quiz.a: The numeric test is true because 05 and 5 have the same integer value. The string test is false because the character strings "05" and "5" differ.

quiz.q: What does ${DIR:-/tmp} produce when DIR is set to an empty string, and when DIR is unset?
quiz.a: Both cases produce /tmp. The :- form uses the default when the variable is unset or empty.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production scripts often rely on shellcheck to catch quoting mistakes before they cause data loss. POSIX parameter expansion adds forms such as ${VAR%pattern} and ${VAR#pattern} for trimming text. Bash arrays and associative arrays handle lists without word-splitting tricks. Newer shells also support set -u to stop on an unset variable. Search for shellcheck, POSIX parameter expansion, and Bash arrays.
